confidence_note: Price versus value via Mr. Market is Graham's central distinction. The 'half-and-half partner' detail and the 'iki yüz' framing in the supplied text are not used. The Buffett attribution is kept only in the sibling story 1783. No quotes are reproduced.
facts: A share has two faces: a price and the value of the underlying business.
Mr. Market names the price every morning; it carries his mood, high when he is euphoric and very low when he is gloomy.
Value reflects what the business actually earns and changes slowly.
Buying a share means becoming a part-owner of a business; the screen price is its daily label.
The investor is not obliged to follow Mr. Market's quote.
When price is far below value, Mr. Market's pessimism becomes an opportunity; far above value, selling can be considered.
Confusing price with value is the trap: the same business is judged good one day and finished the next.
tension: One business carries two numbers, one that shifts every morning and one that barely moves.
opening_idea: Open on the two numbers an investor sees for the same business and the one he must not confuse.

lessons.idea: Keep price and value on separate ledgers before deciding.
lessons.anchor: Mr. Market's daily quote versus what the business earns.

reflect_final: In your last big decision, did the number you saw describe the value of the thing, or someone's mood that day?

use_cases.situation: A team debates buying a fast-rising stock.
use_cases.move: Say the price may be Mr. Market's enthusiasm and ask what the company earns first.

use_cases.situation: An adviser praises a fund's recent rise.
use_cases.move: Ask whether the earnings of the underlying businesses rose as much as the price.

use_cases.situation: You are about to buy a stock whose price fell.
use_cases.move: Ask whether the business changed or only Mr. Market's mood.

pocket_idea: Mr. Market's price is the label; the business under the label is what you buy.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: One business, two numbers: Mr. Market's changes every morning, the business's barely moves.
conversation_variants.thirty_sec_idea: Graham separates price (a mood-driven quote) from value (what the business earns); act when they diverge, never because of the price alone.
